Clown
KLOWN
noun / verb (Gen-Z slang)
From English clown (1500s), first a rustic or boor, then the comic fool of the stage and circus. Gen-Z use took off with the clown-face emoji (added to Unicode in 2016): "I’m a clown" or a row of clown emojis means "I was foolish to believe that," and "clown behaviour" or "clownery" (c. 2018–2019 on Twitter) marks absurd conduct. As a verb, to clown someone is to mock or roast him ("they clowned him for that haircut"), an older African American usage.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang clown does three jobs. Said of oneself, it is a confession: "I’m a clown for thinking he’d text back." Said of another, it is contempt: "that ref is a clown." As a verb, it is mockery: the group chat "clowned" a boy for his shoes. The Christian observation: the first use has a strange dignity, and the third is dangerous. Admitting you were foolish is the beginning of wisdom, and Paul gladly wore the costume for Christ: "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10). David danced before the ark until his wife despised him, and answered, "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight" (2Sa 6:22). But the verb is another matter. The soldiers clowned the King of kings: "they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29). A crown of thorns was their joke. Proverbs says "It is as sport to a fool to do mischief" (Pro 10:23), and God answers mockers in kind: "Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly" (Pro 3:34). A father tells his son: be willing to look like a clown for Christ, and quick to own your own foolishness; but never be the one who clowns another, because the most famous man ever clowned that way was your Lord.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (clown emoji, 2016; "clownery," c. 2018–2019) for a fool, for one’s own foolishness, or for mocking someone — Scripture honours being a fool for Christ (1Co 4:10) and remembers that soldiers clowned the King (Mat 27:29).

CLOWN, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2016–present; emoji and Twitter use) A fool; someone acting absurdly; oneself, for having been gullible. "I’m a clown for believing the test would be easy."

v.t. To clown someone: to mock or roast him. "They clowned him all lunch." Clownery, clown behaviour: absurd conduct. The clown emoji as a self-mocking or contemptuous reply.

Older senses a grandparent knows: a countryman or boor (Shakespeare’s clowns); the comic performer of the circus and stage.

Webster (1828), root word clown: “CLOWN, noun A countryman; a rustic; hence, one who has the manners of a rustic; a churl; a man of coarse manners; an ill-bred man.”

Decode for parents: if your child calls himself a clown, he is admitting a mistake; if he says he clowned someone, ask what was said.

Key Scripture

1Co 4:10 — "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised."

2Sa 6:22 — "And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour."

Mat 27:29 — "And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!"

Pro 10:23 — "It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom."

Pro 3:34 — "Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly."

Modern Corruption

Clown can be an honest confession of foolishness or a costume worn for Christ, but as a verb it is mockery — the very sport the soldiers made of the King of the Jews.

expand to see more

There is a good clown in Scripture. The apostles were treated as the world’s fools and accepted it: "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10). David danced before the LORD with such abandon that Michal despised him, and he said he would be more vile still (2Sa 6:22). A Christian teenager who prays over his lunch or refuses the party may be called a clown; he is in good company. And the self-mocking "I’m a clown" is not far from repentance: the first step out of folly is admitting it.

The verb is the problem. To clown someone is to make him a public joke, and the most infamous clowning in history happened in Pilate’s hall: a robe, a reed for a sceptre, a crown of thorns, and soldiers on their knees saying "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29). The mockers thought it was sport; "It is as sport to a fool to do mischief" (Pro 10:23). God has an answer for scorners: "Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly" (Pro 3:34). Teach your children to laugh at themselves freely and at others carefully, and never to join the crowd that is clowning someone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Probably Scandinavian or Low German (a clod, a lump) → English clown, a rustic (1500s), then a stage fool → 2016 clown emoji → Gen-Z clown, clownery, to clown someone.
